votes.evidence: Part of the premise holds. `resolve_stamphog_acting_reviewer` (products/review_hog/backend/receivers.py:143-156) returns None both when `_resolve_assigned_reviewer` returns None and when the toggle is off. `_resolve_assigned_reviewer` returns None when there is no artefact, when the JSON is bad or not a list, when there are no logins, or when no login resolves to an org member. Stamphog then turns every None into `_InboxCarveOut(opted_out=True)` (products/stamphog/backend/tasks/tasks.py:205-207), and that picks `_INBOX_OPT_OUT_DISMISS_MESSAGE` (tasks.py:897). So the three cases really do share one outcome.
votes.refutation:
The harm the finding claims does not hold up.
(1) The comment is posted only when a stamphog approval is still standing. `_retract_stale_approvals_on_skip` (tasks.py:483-516) returns early when there is no PullRequest row. It posts only through `dismiss_stale_approvals_for_head`, which dismisses approvals that already exist.
(2) An approval can exist only if an earlier review ran, and that review needed resolution to succeed at that moment. So the case needs resolution to break between that approval and a later push, for example the reviewer leaving the org or the artefact being regenerated with no reviewers. That is a narrow timing window.
(3) The claim that the comment "repeats on every push" is wrong. After the first dismissal no approval is left, so later pushes dismiss nothing and post nothing.
(4) The message says "No reviewer currently has stamphog inbox reviews enabled." When no reviewer resolves to an org member, that is still literally true: no resolved reviewer has the toggle on. It is not a false public claim.
(5) The design is documented. The resolver docstring (receivers.py:144) says it returns "the acting reviewer's user id when their stamphog inbox toggle is currently on, else None". The carve-out docstring (tasks.py:157-158) and the message comment (tasks.py:68-69) show the aim was to avoid implying an author-trust problem, and the chosen message does that.
What remains is a small wording point in a rare case, not a defect.

That function (tasks.py:483-516) exits early when there is no PullRequest row, and dismiss_stale_approvals_for_head only acts on a standing approval. So the message goes out only when stamphog approved an earlier head. That earlier approval needed a successful resolution, so the finding's case is a rare change after approval: the reviewer left the org or the artefact was replaced without reviewers. test_tasks.py:796-827 (test_inbox_carve_out_toggle_off_still_dismisses_stale_approvals) covers this dismissal and pins the copy.
votes.refutation:
The claimed public harm doesn't hold up.

1. **The message is literally true.** It says "No reviewer currently has stamphog inbox reviews enabled." When no reviewer resolves to an org member, no resolvable reviewer has the toggle on. What happens next is also right in every case: no re-review, and the stale approval is dismissed. The finding only objects to how the reason is worded.

2. **It does not repeat on every push.** The dismissal only runs when a standing approval exists (tasks.py:483-516, dismiss_stale_approvals_for_head). After the first dismissal there is no approval left, so later pushes post nothing.

3. **The trigger is narrow.** Stamphog must first have approved through a successful resolution. Then the reviewer must leave the org, or the artefact must be regenerated without reviewers, before the next push. The generic fallback message ("This PR no longer qualifies for automatic review") would not be clearer for the user either.

This is a wording preference on a rare path, not a correctness defect.

votes.evidence:
The code path the finding describes does exist. `resolve_stamphog_acting_reviewer` (products/review_hog/backend/receivers.py:144-156) returns None in three cases: `_resolve_assigned_reviewer` finds nothing (no artefact at :186-187, bad JSON or no logins at :188-199, no login maps to an org member at :202-205), or the toggle is off (:154-155). The carve-out at products/stamphog/backend/tasks/tasks.py:205-207 turns every one of those Nones into `opted_out=True`. The skip path at tasks.py:893-898 then picks `_INBOX_OPT_OUT_DISMISS_MESSAGE` (tasks.py:70-74).

Two facts limit when this runs in production:
1. The message is only posted when a stale approval is actually dismissed. `_retract_stale_approvals_on_skip` (tasks.py:483-509) returns early if there is no PullRequest row, and otherwise calls `dismiss_stale_approvals_for_head` on existing approvals.
2. A stamphog approval on a self-driving PR needs an earlier review, and that review needed the same resolver to succeed with the toggle on (receivers.py:111-139 for the first review, tasks.py:204-215 for later pushes).

So the only trigger is resolution breaking mid-PR after an approval was granted. That means the acting reviewer leaves the org or unlinks their GitHub login, or the latest suggested_reviewers artefact is regenerated with no reviewer that resolves. It can happen, but the window is narrow and it depends on org-membership changes. The PR is bot-authored (tasks.py:176-179), so no human "PR author" reads a false claim about themselves.
votes.refutation:
The message is not false in the cases the finding names. It says "No reviewer currently has stamphog inbox reviews enabled for this self-driving PR, so stamphog will not re-review" (tasks.py:70-74). It never says anyone opted out. If no reviewer login maps to an org member (receivers.py:202-205), or the latest artefact has no reviewers (:186-200), then no current reviewer has the toggle on. The statement is literally true, and "will not re-review" is also accurate.

The other message, `_UNTRUSTED_SKIP_DISMISS_MESSAGE` (tasks.py:63-66), would be less accurate here. The comment at tasks.py:68-69 says it wrongly implies an author-trust problem for an identified self-driving PR. The "fix" would replace a roughly correct message with a misleading one.

The trigger is also narrow. It needs an approval that already exists, plus a reviewer who later leaves the org or an artefact that is regenerated. The cost is wording on a bot-authored PR comment. Retracting the approval still happens either way, so there is no correctness or safety impact. At most this is a preference about wording, not a defect.
